references.text: Continues the same law regarding injury to slaves; here it concerns a tooth instead of an eye, with the same principle of release as compensation.
The law of retaliation (lex talionis) establishing the principle of 'eye for eye,' which is the background for this slave law.
Repeats the principle of 'eye for eye,' showing the legal context for protection against mutilation.
Earlier legislation concerning the release of Hebrew slaves, establishing the context for the release of slaves in verse 26.
Laws regarding the treatment of Israelite slaves and foreign slaves, elaborating on slave legislation.
Rules for the release of Hebrew slaves, showing the connection to release as compensation.
Job acknowledges that slaves have rights against their master, reflecting the principle in Exodus 21:26.
Complementary rules in the same legal code: murder requires vengeance, while permanent injury to a slave requires release as restitution.
Principles of restitution for bodily harm: temporary injury requires payment, while permanent injury to a slave requires release.
Comparison of liability: direct violence by the owner grants the slave freedom, while injury caused by an animal requires financial compensation to the owner.
General principle (Lev 24:19) meets specific application (Ex 21:26): freedom as restitution for an eye instead of physical retaliation.
